title: Drag as Evidence: Motion-Grounded Latent Recomposition for Drag-Based Editing
claim: Existing methods either miss the specified motion or distort natural appearance; ours follows the motion while keeping realistic structure.
layout: 2 rows by 8 columns, left-to-right, ours highlighted in blue box
description: A grid of image examples with two rows (a lion roaring, a person holding a crocodile) and eight columns. Column headers are grouped by braces: Inputs (Point Input with red/blue drag points and arrows, and Warped Image with a white inpainting mask and a crudely warped subject), Existing drag-based methods (DragDiffusion, FastDrag, Inpaint4Drag), a Text-based method (Longcat-Image-Edit), and Ours (MoRe-Drag). The last column is set apart in a light blue rounded box with blue italic header text, so the eye lands on it. Baseline headers are gray. Baseline outputs show blur, artifacts, or weak motion following. The MoRe-Drag outputs show a sharp lion mouth and a crocodile with a realistically opened jaw. Drag handles are drawn on the images.
caption: Editing comparison. Pixel-space warping provides explicit but imperfect motion evidence. MoRe-Drag injects this evidence into the generative trajectory, enabling the editor to follow the specified motion while restoring natural structure and appearance.
abstract: Modern image editors excel at semantic manipulation and visual synthesis, yet remain limited in precise spatial control, motivating the development of drag-based editing. However, existing drag-based methods often struggle to balance drag accuracy with natural, plausible, and intent-aligned generation. We propose MoRe-Drag, a motion-grounded drag-based editing method. Our key insight is to treat pixel-space warping as coarse motion evidence, and to inject this evidence into the generative sampling trajectory. Specifically, MoRe-Drag performs region-aware latent recomposition over refinement, inpainting, and preservation regions, coupled with stage-adaptive conditioning that progressively shifts from motion-grounded structure formation to semantic refinement. We further support a no-manual-instruction interface by adapting the MLLM-based text encoder for drag-aware instruction inference. Experiments on DragBench-SR and DragBench-DR show that MoRe-Drag substantially improves drag precision over strong base editors and achieves superior drag accuracy among SOTA drag-based methods, while delivering strong semantic consistency and visually realistic results. Project page: https://xinyu-pu.github.io/projects/more-drag/.
